# Release post in the company's voice

Read a release's engineering notes and the company's style guide for release posts, and return the customer-facing blog post a product marketing manager pastes into the CMS: the title, slug, meta description, excerpt, category and tags, each held to the guide's limits, the body in Markdown written to the guide's rules, and what the post leaves out of the notes, with the rule that leaves it out, to check before publishing.

`github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3` · [bundle.mthds](bundle.mthds)

## The sample

**Sample release notes**

> ### [0.7.0] - 2026-09-23
>
> #### Added
>
> - **`pipelex-catalog` — a bundle directory and the organization's Pipelex catalog, in one skill.** Three gestures and no fourth: list what the API key's organization has saved (server-side search, paged), save a directory — a creation when it carries no `pipelex-method.json` link, an update of the method that link names when it does — and pull a saved method's files back to disk into `methods/<name>/`, by the same project-shape rule `/pipelex-design` uses — the method-app stop included, since `make add-method` writes the action trio, the narrower and the registry entry a plain write would leave unwritten — with `<name>` folded into one directory segment rather than spelled from the catalog's free text, so a name carrying a separator never contributes a path, and with `output_dir` expressed relative to the workshop's own working directory, which is where the workshop writes. The save is one call that reads the files, validates them and stores those same bytes, so a verdict taken separately is never worth its second read: an invalid bundle comes back as a verdict with nothing saved anywhere and routes to `/pipelex-edit` or `/pipelex-design`, and a valid bundle with pending signatures is saved with the statement that it does not run yet. Before an update the skill says in one line what an update is — a deployment every caller of that id, a production call site included, picks up on its next call — and the user's request is the consent, so nothing here ever saves on its own initiative and no other skill saves at all. It refuses to overwrite what it has not seen: a save carrying the link's `synced_updated_at` is stopped when the saved method has moved, with both timestamps and two ways forward that the skill never picks between, and a pull into a linked directory whose files differ either stops (local work the catalog never got) or asks before overwriting (the saved method moved, and the link records no hashes to say whose change it is). Which `.py` files are the method's is the skill's judgement and never a sweep of the directory — a `function_name` is a key in the runtime's flat function registry and names no file, so the set is read from the bundle's own Python — the file defining each registered function and the bundle files it imports — nothing at all when the bundle holds no `PipeFunc`, and the clearing `python: []` only on request. A create is never retried after a transport fault, because the idempotency key the platform honours cannot be sent yet and a retry mints a second method; deletion is not offered at all and is named as the webapp's, since it is admin-only and erases every run the method produced. The skill writes no file itself: the pulled sources and the `pipelex-method.json` link are the workshop's to write, which is why the only tool it pre-approves that can touch the filesystem is `Bash(git status:*)`: hand-writing a link file, or removing a dead one, stops for the user instead of recording the wrong plane. `/pipelex-design` and `/pipelex-edit` each gained one sentence pointing here.
> - **`pipelex-design`, `pipelex-edit` and `pipelex-organize` take a registered method's catalog id.** They work on files, so an `mt_…` id is resolved to a directory first: one search over the `pipelex-method.json` link files finds the directory already linked to that method, and where there is none the pull is handed to `/pipelex-catalog`. Two hits are the user's choice rather than the first match, since a comparison copy carries the same link, and a published address is refused with a pointer to `/pipelex-explain`, there being nowhere to write a change back.
> - **The three file-based skills say when the saved copy has fallen behind.** A report from a directory carrying a link now names the linked method and says the catalog still holds what it held before the change, so every caller of that id goes on running the old content. It offers `/pipelex-catalog` and never saves: a save is a deployment, and no skill but that one makes it.
> - **A run of a linked bundle directory is filed under its saved method.** `pipelex-run` reads the link and sends its `method_id` beside the `files`, so the run appears in that method's history in the webapp — the files are what ran, which the report says plainly. A linkage id the plane does not know refuses the run before anything executes, reported with the host the link records and with the offer of the same run without the id.
>
> #### Changed
>
> - **`pipelex-integrate` installs `pipelex-sdk` 0.10.2 for a Python consumer.** The floor the skill states and raises an older pin to now matches what `pipelex-starter-python` declares, so the reference project's code — its blocking mode reads a run through the SDK's `results_from_execute` — runs on what the skill installed. Everything the generated call site and the offline drift gate use was already there; the floor follows the reference so the two cannot drift apart.
> - **`pipelex-explain` reads a saved method's source instead of describing its contract.** A catalog id names the organization's own method, so the skill fetches its files through the workshop's inline read — never the arm that writes to disk — and explains them exactly as a bundle on disk, the stored Python included. A bounded read makes the explanation partial rather than the library incomplete, and where that tool is not served the id falls back to contract level, which is a narrower explanation and not a stop. A published address is unchanged: its internals stay in the repository it names.
> - **`pipelex-run` names a missing `PipeFunc` implementation as the cause of a failure rather than a suspect.** A `files` submission carries `.mthds` only, and a linked run resolves nothing from the catalog, so a bundle whose `PipeFunc` names a function the hosted plane does not already have registered has no channel for its Python on any run from files. The cure the skill gives is `/pipelex-catalog`: a saved method run by its id alone has its `.mthds` and `.py` assembled into the run bundle server-side.

**Sample style guide**

> Blog style guide for release posts: written for a Pipelex example; it is not Pipelex's own style guide.
>
> We publish a post on the company blog for every release of the Pipelex plugin that changes what our users can do. The post turns the engineering release notes into something a user reads in three minutes and acts on. Every rule below applies to every post.
>
> Who reads it
>
> 1. Our readers build and run methods with the Pipelex plugin in their coding agent, whether Claude Code, Codex or Mistral Vibe: developers, and the business teams who work with them. They know what a method is and what the plugin does. They do not know our internal file names, our tools' permission settings, or how we build, test and release the plugin.
>
> What goes in, and what stays out
>
> 2. Write about what the reader can now do, or will now see happen, that they could not before. Group the notes by what the reader does, not by the notes' Added, Changed and Fixed headings: several notes about one feature make one section.
> 3. Leave out whatever does not change what the reader does: how we build, test and release; the configuration and link files the tools write for the reader; permission settings; retry and idempotency logic; the version of a library the plugin installs, unless the reader must do something about it; and the reasons behind an implementation choice.
> 4. When a feature protects the reader, for instance by asking before it overwrites something or by never acting on its own, say so in one plain sentence, as a benefit.
> 5. Say what a feature does not do only when a reader would otherwise look for it there, and say where to go instead.
> 6. Promise nothing the notes do not say: no dates, no roadmap, no prices, and no figures the notes do not give.
>
> How it reads
>
> 7. Speak as "we" for the company and "you" for the reader. Use plain words, active verbs and the present tense. Write in American English.
> 8. No hype: never "revolutionary", "seamless", "game-changing", "supercharge", "unlock", "effortless" or "powerful". No exclamation marks and no rhetorical questions.
> 9. Name a skill by its slash command in code format the first time it appears, then by what it does. Write commands, identifiers and file names in code format.
> 10. The first paragraph says, in at most 60 words, what the reader can now do, and names the release by the product's name and its version number.
>
> The structure of the post
>
> 11. An opening paragraph, as rule 10 says; then one section for each thing the reader can now do, each under a level-2 heading in sentence case that starts with a verb; then a section headed "Also in this release", with one bullet of one sentence for each smaller change worth a reader's attention; then a section headed "Get the update", holding this sentence as it stands: "Update the Pipelex plugin in your coding agent to get these changes; the release notes list every change."
> 12. The body runs to 400 to 700 words. It carries no title of its own, since the CMS prints the title above it.
>
> The fields the CMS takes
>
> 13. Title: sentence case, at most 60 characters, naming the product and the main change, with no version number.
> 14. Slug: the title's key words in lowercase, joined by hyphens, at most six words, with no version number.
> 15. Meta description: one sentence of 120 to 155 characters saying what the reader can now do.
> 16. Excerpt: at most 200 characters, shown on the blog's index page and in the newsletter.
> 17. Category: Product updates.
> 18. Tags: three to five of these, and no others: Pipelex plugin, Claude Code, Codex, Mistral Vibe, Methods, Catalog, Integrations, SDK.

*Written for this example.* Licence: [MIT](https://github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/blob/main/LICENSE). Credit: Evotis S.A.S.

**`meta_description`**

List, save, and pull your organization’s methods, work by catalog ID, track linked runs, and explain saved methods from source.

**`excerpt`**

Manage your organization’s saved methods from your coding agent, use catalog IDs across skills, track linked runs, and explain stored source.

**`tags`**

- Pipelex plugin
- Methods
- Catalog

**`body`**

In Pipelex plugin 0.7.0, you can list, save, and pull your organization’s methods from your coding agent, work with saved methods by catalog ID, track linked runs in method history, and explain saved methods from their source.

### Manage methods in your catalog

Use `/pipelex-catalog` to manage the methods saved by the organization associated with your API key. You can search and page through saved methods, save a bundle directory as a new method or an update, and pull a saved method’s files into `methods/<name>/`.

The catalog skill validates a bundle before saving it. It does not save an invalid bundle and directs you to `/pipelex-edit` or `/pipelex-design` to correct it. You can save a valid bundle with pending signatures, but it does not run until those signatures are complete.

Updating a saved method is a deployment. Every caller using that method ID, including a production call site, receives the updated content on its next call. The catalog skill saves only when you request it, and no other skill saves methods to the catalog.

The skill also protects your work from conflicting changes. It stops a save if the catalog copy has changed since you last saw it and gives you two ways to proceed without choosing for you. When you pull, it stops if you have local work that was never saved or asks before overwriting when the saved method has also changed.

Deletion is not available through the catalog skill. An admin must delete a method in the webapp, and deletion erases every run that method produced. The design and editing skills direct you to the catalog skill when you need to save your work.

### Work with saved methods by catalog ID

The design and editing skills, along with `/pipelex-organize`, now accept an `mt_…` catalog ID. If the method already has a local directory, the skill works with that copy. Otherwise, it hands the pull to the catalog skill. If two local copies match the same method, the skill asks you to choose instead of selecting one.

These file-based skills also report when local changes have left the catalog copy behind. The report names the saved method and explains that callers using its ID still run the older catalog content. The skills direct you to the catalog skill to deploy your changes and never save them automatically.

You cannot change a published address through these file-based skills. Use `/pipelex-explain` instead.

### Track linked runs in method history

`/pipelex-run` now files a run from a linked bundle directory under its saved method in the webapp. The report makes clear that the submitted local files are what ran.

If the saved method ID is unknown, the run stops before executing anything. This prevents the run from being associated with an invalid method, and you can choose to run the same files without that association.

### Explain saved methods from their source

The explanation skill now accepts the catalog ID of a method saved by your organization. It reads and explains the stored bundle files, including Python, instead of describing only the method’s contract. It reads the source without writing those files to disk.

If it cannot read all the stored source, the explanation can be partial. If source reading is unavailable, the skill returns a narrower contract-level explanation instead of stopping.

Published addresses do not receive source-level explanations through this skill. Their internal source remains in the repository named by the address.

### Also in this release

- The run skill now identifies a missing `PipeFunc` implementation as the cause of a file-based run failure and directs you to the catalog skill so the saved method can run with its `.mthds` and `.py` files.

### Get the update

Update the Pipelex plugin in your coding agent to get these changes; the release notes list every change.

**Takes**

- `release_notes`, a text (`ReleaseNotes`): The notes of one release as engineering writes them, for developers: every change of the release, with the mechanics behind it.
- `style_guide`, a text (`StyleGuide`): The company's written style guide for release posts: who reads them, what goes in and what stays out, the voice, the structure of a post and the fields the blog's CMS takes.

**Returns** a `ReleasePost`: A release post ready to paste into the blog's CMS, with what it leaves out of the release notes for the manager to check before publishing.

- `title`, text: The post's title.
- `slug`, text: The post's URL slug.
- `meta_description`, text: The description search engines show under the title.
- `excerpt`, text: The short summary shown on the blog's index page and in the newsletter.
- `category`, text: The post's category.
- `tags`, a list of texts: The post's tags.
- `body`, text: The body of the post in Markdown, as the CMS takes it.
- `left_out`, a list of `LeftOutNote`: What the post leaves out of the release notes, each with the style guide's rule that leaves it out.

With the Pipelex MCP in ChatGPT or Claude ([add it once](https://github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-mcp)), ask:

```text
Run github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3 with the sample inputs in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.3/methods/write_release_post/inputs.json
```

In Claude Code or Codex with the [Pipelex plugin](https://github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-plugins), the same sentence runs through `/pipelex-run`.

## Put it in your code

Each call runs the method on the hosted API with your `PIPELEX_API_KEY` ([create one](https://app.pipelex.com)).

The sample inputs are too long to write out here, so each snippet below fetches them from the method's [`inputs.json`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.3/methods/write_release_post/inputs.json).

<details>
<summary>TypeScript</summary>

```bash
npm install @pipelex/sdk
```

```ts
import { PipelexApiClient } from "@pipelex/sdk";

const response = await fetch("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.3/methods/write_release_post/inputs.json");
const inputs = (await response.json()) as Record<string, unknown>;
const client = new PipelexApiClient({ apiKey: process.env.PIPELEX_API_KEY });
const result = await client.startAndWaitForResult({
  method_ref: "github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3",
  inputs,
});
console.log(result.main_stuff);
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Python</summary>

```bash
pip install pipelex-sdk
```

```python
import asyncio

import httpx
from pipelex_sdk.client import PipelexAPIClient


async def main() -> None:
    inputs = httpx.get("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.3/methods/write_release_post/inputs.json").json()
    async with PipelexAPIClient() as client:
        result = await client.start_and_wait(
            method_ref="github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3",
            inputs=inputs,
        )
        print(result.main_stuff)


asyncio.run(main())
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Any HTTP client</summary>

The start call answers at once with the run's id, or with the reason it refused the run; the results call answers 202 while the run is going, 200 with the results once it has completed, and 409 if it failed. The snippet uses `jq` to wrap the sample inputs into the start call's body and to read the id.

```bash
START=$(curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.3/methods/write_release_post/inputs.json |
  jq -c '{method_ref: "github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3", inputs: .}' |
  curl -s https://api.pipelex.com/v1/start \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIPELEX_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d @-)
RUN_ID=$(printf '%s' "$START" | jq -r '.pipeline_run_id // empty')
if [ -z "$RUN_ID" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$START"; else
  until [ "$(curl -s -o results.json -w '%{http_code}' https://api.pipelex.com/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/results \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIPELEX_API_KEY")" != 202 ]; do sleep 5; done
  cat results.json
fi
```

</details>

In a project you already have, ask your agent for `/pipelex-integrate github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3`: it generates the result's types and writes one typed call.

## Make it an app

```bash
npm create @pipelex/method-app@latest release-post-app -- --method github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3
make -C release-post-app serve
```

The form and the result view come from the method's contract. `make serve` prints the app's URL once the page answers, and `make stop` stops it. Your agent does the same with `/pipelex-scaffold`.

## Make it yours

Ask your agent:

```text
Copy github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3 into ./release-post, add a social post of at most 280 characters announcing the release in the style guide's voice, beside the blog post, prove it on the sample, and save it to my Pipelex account.
```

From then on every door above takes your method's id (`mt_…`) in place of the address, and your chatbot lists it among your methods.

## Run it on your own machine

With the Pipelex runtime and your own provider keys ([set it up](https://docs.pipelex.com/latest/get-started/run-it-yourself/)):

```bash
curl -sLo inputs.json https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/v0.20.3/methods/write_release_post/inputs.json
pipelex run method github.com/Pipelex/pipelex-cookbook/write_release_post@v0.20.3 --inputs inputs.json
```
